records.title: Dr. Strangelove Or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
records.description:
Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1964. 95 mins. 35mm. With Peter Sellers, George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Slim Pickens, Keenan Wynn. Stanley Kubrick reinvents the nuclear suspense thriller, then in vogue, as an absurdist black comedy in this brilliant evocation of cold war paranoia.
Dr. Strangelove,
co-written by Kubrick and Terry Southern, strikes just the right manic, irreverent, sexually charged tone, creating a satirical masterpiece that is one of the seminal counterculture works of the 1960s. Towering over the cast—which also includes George C. Scott as the blustering General Buck Turgidson and Sterling Hayden as “precious bodily fluids”–obsessed General Jack D. Ripper—is Sellers, a triple threat as meek RAF Captain Mandrake, bungling U.S. President Merkin Muffley, and, of course, the mad scientist title character—inventor of the doomsday machine that may wipe out humanity as we know it.

records.title: The Long, Long Trailer
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1953, 96 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Lucille Ball, Desi Arnaz, Marjorie Main, Keenan Wynn. Lucy and Desi
and
Minnelli? Talk about a dream team. In this hilarious mix of romantic comedy, slapstick, and suspense, Ball and Arnaz—at the time the two most popular performers in the nation—play Tacy and Nicky (of course), an engaged couple who purchase a trailer so they can journey the country and play at domesticity before tying the knot. Aside from getting to see America’s favorite redhead in Technicolor,
The Long, Long Trailer,
the only major big-screen outing for the TV icons, offers up the perfect premise for a 1950s comedy, commenting on the comforts of postwar material culture with escalating madcap brilliance.

records.title: Hold Onto Me
records.description:
Dir. Myrsini Aristidou. 2026, 102 mins. Greece. DCP. In Greek with English subtitles. With Maria Petrova, Christos Passalis, Jenny Sallo. It’s summer, and plucky 11-year-old Iris is running wild through the streets with her friend Danae when she discovers that her estranged father, Aris, is back in town for his father’s funeral. Determined to know him, Iris tracks him down to a dilapidated shipyard, where he’s been keeping to himself. What begins as a stubborn attempt to reconnect slowly unfolds into a fragile, imperfect, yet poignant bond.
Hold Onto Me
won the Sundance 2026 Audience Award in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition and is the first-ever Cyprus submission for the Best International Feature Oscar. Christos Passalis won the 2026 New York Greek Film Expo Award for Best Performance by an Actor.

records.title: The Cobweb
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1955, 134 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Lauren Bacall, Richard Widmark, Gloria Grahame, Lillian Gish, Charles Boyer, John Kerr, Susan Strasberg, Oscar Levant. An essential Minnelli, featuring maybe his most wildly stacked cast,
The Cobweb
confidently offers up a nearly undefinable mix of the restrained and the truly eccentric. Set in a psychiatric hospital, where the staff is likely more unsettled than the patients, this Cinemascope, Eastmancolor contraption details the fallout after the head doctor’s wife does the unthinkable: she changes the color of the library’s drapes! Long read as a perfect auteur text for Minnelli (who got his start as a window dresser),
The Cobweb
is a gorgeously shot, low-boil soap opera that’s a must for any 1950s melodrama completist.

records.title: Lolita
records.description:
Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1962. 152 mins. 35mm. With James Mason, Shelley Winters, Peter Sellers, Sue Lyon. “How did they ever make a movie of
Lolita
?” the savvy, shocked poster tagline wondered. Only Stanley Kubrick would dare try. Outwitting the censors, Kubrick turned Vladimir Nabokov’s 1955 novel about a professor’s obsession with a young “nymphet” into a rich cinematic satire, emphasizing Nabokov’s dark social comedy. A monstrously proper James Mason is unforgettable as Humbert Humbert, whose twisted heart leads him to destroy his own life and soul for the love of the teenage daughter (Sue Lyon) of his crass and lovelorn landlady (Shelley Winters). As the mysterious oddball playwright Clare Quilty, Sellers lends Kubrick’s tragic satire a coherent sense of eccentricity and outlandish humor.

records.title: The Muppets Take Manhattan + The Muppet Show with Liza Minnelli
records.description:
Dir. Frank Oz. U.S., 1984, 94 mins. U.S. DCP. With Jim Henson, Dave Goelz, Jerry Nelson, Richard Hunt, Steve Whitmire, Liza Minnelli. When the Muppets’ college revue is a big hit, they decide to take the show all the way to Broadway. Adjusting to the hustle and bustle of New York City, Kermit takes a job at a local restaurant while he searches for a producer. Filled with cameos by quintessential New Yorkers, such as Gregory Hines, Joan Rivers, James Coco, Brooke Shields, and Liza Minnelli, the movie ends with a fantastical and questionably genuine wedding between Kermit and Miss Piggy. Oz’s first solo-directed film is a dose of pure joy, a true gift to showtune lovers featuring some of the greatest songs in the Muppet canon and the beloved “Muppet Babies” sequence that spawned its own mini-franchise. records.title: Paths of Glory
records.description:
Preceded by Kubrick’s documentary short
The Seafarers
(1953, 30 mins)
Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1957. 88 mins. 35mm. With Kirk Douglas, Ralph Meeker, Adolphe Menjou, George Macready, Wayne Morris, Richard Anderson. One of the bleakest anti-war films ever made, Stanley Kubrick’s brilliant World War I drama about the abuse of military hierarchy drives home its message in every aspect of its construction, from its mechanized tracking shots through trenches to its disturbingly protracted climax.
Paths of Glory
represents the first full expression of Kubrick’s style, but it also is the last of his films to center around a wholly virtuous hero (Douglas) and the last to view the human individual as a bulwark of decency in an inhuman world.

records.title: The Year of Living Dangerously
records.description:
Dir. Peter Weir. 1983, 115 mins. Australia/U.S./Philippines. 35mm. With Mel Gibson, Sigourney Weaver, Linda Hunt. Bembol Rocco, Michael Murphy. Operating at the height of his storytelling powers, and following his international successes with
Picnic at Hanging Rock
and
Gallipoli
,
Australian director Peter Weir took a big swing with this sweeping yet intimate historical drama. Set in Indonesia in the mid-sixties in the lead-up to the overthrow of President Sukarno’s government, Weir’s adaptation of Christopher Koch’s acclaimed novel centers around an Australian journalist (Gibson) and his romantic relationship with a British embassy officer (Weaver) and his professional one with a Chinese Australian photojournalist (Hunt, in an Oscar-winning performance). Suspenseful, romantic, and intelligent, the film predicted Weir’s remarkable run in Hollywood, yet stands on its own as a singular 1980s entertainment that traffics in politically complex themes with nuance and depth.

records.title: Demons
records.description:
Dir. Lamberto Bava. 1985, 88 min. DCP. With Natasha Hovey, Michele Soavi, Paolo Cazzo, Urbano Barberini, Karl Zinny. While attending the premiere of a horror movie, friends Cheryl (Hovey) and Kathy (Cazzo) find themselves trapped in the cinema from hell. Reality begins to imitate the film on the screen as members of the audience transform into ravenous demons and go on the rampage. A collaboration by producer Dario Argento and director Lamberto Bava,
Demons
is a marvel of bloody special effects by two Italian horror maestros that satirizes the idea that the Devil is lurking in every corner of the pop culture young people consume, waiting to corrupt and possess them.

records.title: Side Street
records.description:
Dir. Anthony Mann. 1949, 83 mins. 35mm. With Farley Granger, Cathy O’Donnell, James Craig. A part-time letter carrier foolishly steals $30,000 from gangsters and is soon on the run from them and the police. Mann returned to the city of his youth to direct this shattering film noir that reunites Granger with
They Live by Night
co-star Cathy O’Donnell. Following in the post-World War II tradition of such semi-documentary thrillers as
The Naked City,
Side Street
makes spectacular use of New York locations as the tortured protagonist wanders everywhere from Midtown to Greenwich Village, from South Street Seaport to skid row, culminating in a gripping (and symbolic) car chase through the financial district.

records.title: A Fox Under a Pink Moon
records.description:
Dir. Mehrdad Oskouei & Soraya. 2025, 96 mins. Iran, Turkey, Greece. DCP. In Farsi with English subtitles.
A moving, artful, and surprising collaboration between the legendary Iranian filmmaker Mehrdad Oskouei and a whip-smart teenage artist,
A Fox Under a Pink Moon
follows Afghani refugee Soraya’s relentless efforts to escape an abusive marriage in Tehran and join her mother in Austria. But rather than the cliché frame of master and muse, Oskouei remotely directed Soraya to tell her own story, from both her reality and her imagination. In addition to many attempts to cross the border into Europe, Soraya escapes and resists oppression through her dark and unfettered artwork, which often features an enigmatic fox and weeping clown. It is her work that gives the film its shape and aching intimacy, from the watercolor animations derived from her drawings, to her smartphone video diaries tracking five years of survival separated from her home and loving family. Poetic and raw,
A Fox Under a Pink Moon
is as electric and courageous as its heroine, making it easy to see why this film won awards all over the world and is in serious discussion for the 2027 Oscars Awards.

records.title: Gigi
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1958, 115 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Leslie Caron, Louis Jourdan, Maurice Chevalier, Hermione Gingold. The CinemaScope frame is crammed with exquisite detail in this thrillingly visualized musical adapted from a story by Collette about a girl’s coming-of-age in wealthy turn-of-the-century Paris. Minnelli’s film is both tender and sly, a social satire of sexual mores as well as a moving tale of an innocent’s entrance into a complicated world in which women’s options are limited. The winner of nine Oscars (a record at the time), including Best Picture, Director, Cinematography, Art Direction, Costume Design, Song, and Score (by
My Fair Lady
composers Lerner and Loewe),
Gigi
is a triumph on every level, like a Toulouse-Lautrec painting sprung to giddy life.

records.title: The Muppet Christmas Carol: The Uncut Version
records.description:
Dir. Brian Henson. 1992, 85 mins. U.S. DCP. With Michael Caine, Dave Goelz, Steve Whitmire, Jerry Nelson, Frank Oz. In this beloved staple of many a childhood, the Charles Dickens classic is recast with the classic Muppet characters, including Gonzo as Charles Dickens, Kermit at Bob Cratchit, and Fozzie Bear as Fozziwig. This faithful adaptation is as full of Christmas spirit and imagination as any of the various film adaptations of the novel, and features a towering performance by Caine as the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge and a splendid musical score by Paul Williams. This full, uncut version of the original release features the song “When Love Is Gone.”

records.title: Bells Are Ringing
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1960, 126 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Judy Holliday, Dean Martin, Fred Clark, Jean Stapleton. In his delightful musical pairing with Oscar-winner Judy Holliday and superstar Dean Martin, Minnelli directs an effervescent New York–set romantic comedy about a nosy Brooklyn telephone operator for an answering service who finds herself falling for a poor wannabe playwright while also trying to play matchmaker to her other clients. With her tender, metropolitan vivaciousness, Holliday is as note-perfect as always, while the film is also a showcase for the musical talents of composers Betty Comden and Adolph Green, from whose Broadway hit the show is adapted.
Bells Are Ringing
would be the final musical from the famed MGM Freed Unit, and earned Minnelli a DGA nomination for Best Director.

records.title: Barry Lyndon
records.description:
Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1975. 184 mins. DCP. With Ryan O’Neal, Marisa Berenson, Patrick Magee, Hardy Krüger, Diane Koerner, Gay Hamilton, Leon Vitali. William Makepeace Thackeray’s picaresque classic novel becomes, in Kubrick’s hands, a historical epic that has the visual texture and scope of Hogarth and Gainsborough canvases. O’Neal is the opportunistic Irish cad who fakes his way into nobility, however briefly, while Berenson and Vitali expertly inhabit his wife and stepson—the latter who will prove to be his undoing. Both large-scale epic and intimate domestic drama,
Barry Lyndon
is a work of magisterial tragicomedy that was misunderstood upon its release but is now rightly considered one of the director’s great masterworks. Winner of four Academy Awards, including cinematography, art direction, costume design, and adapted score.

records.title: Father of the Bride
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1950, 92 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Spencer Tracy, Elizabeth Taylor, Joan Bennett, Don Taylor, Billie Burke. Forty years before it was remade into another beloved comedy starring Steve Martin and Diane Keaton, Minnelli’s sparkling original
Father of the Bride
delighted audiences with its perfect mix of caustic comedy and sentiment. A superb Spencer Tracy stars as strait-laced businessman Stanley Banks, whose life unravels when the apple of his eye (a teenage Elizabeth Taylor) announces she’s getting married. With its pointed satire of perfect postwar suburbia and clever portrait of a well-intentioned but disgruntled family man sent to the edge of sanity by the trappings—and out-of-control cost—of putting on a good(bye) show for his daughter, the Best Picture–nominated
Father of the Bride
kicked off the 1950s in smart, funny style and remains a treasure of its era.

Bill, torn between his adoration of a beautiful dancer (Leslie Caron) and his pragmatic need for the attention of an elegant arts patron (Nina Foch). is pure cinematic bliss and a musical movie landmark filled with such Gershwin gems as “I Got Rhythm,” “’S Wonderful,” “Our Love Is Here to Stay” and “I’ll Build a Stairway to Paradise.”

records.title: Brigadoon

Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1954, 108 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Gene Kelly, Cyd Charisse, Van Johnson, Elaine Stewart. One of the first Cinemascope, Technicolor musicals, this MGM extravaganza, adapted from the stage by the great Lerner and Loewe, is an enchanting fantasy in which a pair of New Yorkers find themselves in a magical Scottish town called Brigadoon, which only materializes once every hundred years. Brigadoon
is a poignant supernatural romance about the aching ephemerality of existence.

This madcap New York City farce stars Dudley Moore as an alcoholic playboy man-child who has lived off the millions inherited from his parents and has never had to work a day in his life. Dir. Martin Scorsese. 1977, 164 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Robert De Niro, Liza Minnelli, Lionel Stander. Scorsese’s ode to classic MGM musicals and 1940s jazz marked a departure for him, combining his gritty hard-boiled realism (he had just made

Undoubtedly one of the director’s masterworks, the film brilliantly depicts the difficulty of a marriage between two independent creatives, and Scorsese pushes the story of the doomed relationship between a jazz singer and a saxophonist into dark, exhilarating territory. The final half hour, when Scorsese gives the film over to pure movie musical magic, makes for one of his most sustained feats of grand filmmaking, while Minnelli’s climactic belting of the now-classic title song (written by Fred Ebb and John Kander for the film) is a true showstopper.

Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1953, 111 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Fred Astaire, Cyd Charisse, Oscar Levant, Nanette Fabray, Jack Buchanan. One of the crowning glories of American musical cinema, Minnelli’s
The Band Wagon

Playing a version of himself as an aging Hollywood star, Astaire leads a cast that includes Fabray and Levant, standing in for the film’s real-life writers Betty Comden and Adolph Green; Buchanan, incarnating a pretentious, blowhard actor-director à la Orson Welles; and Charisse, playing the ballet dancer turned show business ingénue she then was.
The Band Wagon
elevates these Hollywood traditions to new heights of technical display (“A Shine on Your Shoes”), self-reflexive comedy (“That’s Entertainment!”), and sublime visual poetry (“Dancing in the Dark”).

co-curators Michelle Finamore and Emma Cormack.

records.title: Pinball (with director Naveen Chaubal in person)
records.description:
With director Naveen Chaubal and producer Bryn Silverman in person
Dir. Naveen Chaubal. 2026, 86 mins. U.S. DCP. In English, Arabic with English subtitles. In this tender coming of age portrait, Yosef, a spirited athlete in Louisville, Kentucky, contemplates his past as a displaced Iraqi refugee, his present as an immigrant trying to make sense of his kaleidoscopic identity, and his uncertain future. As Yosef reaches milestones of adulthood—high school graduation, his sister’s departure from the U.S.—long-buried questions come to the surface: where does he belong? Has he truly escaped from the shadow of war? What does it mean to build a future in a place shaped by the same forces that displaced his family? Is the life he is living truly his own—or simply the safest one available to him? In director Naveen Chaubal’s feature documentary debut, Yosef dives into the memories of his journey from Iraq to America and, like the steel ball ricocheting inside a machine, navigates shifting social, cultural, political, and financial pressures, trying to find stillness, purpose, and a place to land in an increasingly chaotic world.

records.title: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
records.description:
With filmmaker Matías Piñeiro in person
The screening will be preceded by a book signing with Piñeiro at 3:00 p.m.
Dir. John Ford. 1962, 123 mins. U.S. 35mm. With James Stewart, John Wayne, Lee Marvin, Woody Strode. Who shot the vicious outlaw Liberty Valance? Was it the law-and-order senator (James Stewart), representing the new order, or the rugged gunman (John Wayne), representing the pioneer tradition? There are no easy answers in this twilight western that serves as John Ford’s profound summation and reevaluation of his earlier movies and features Wayne and Stewart in two of their greatest late-career roles. The film that coined the phrase “When the legend becomes fact, print the legend,”
The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
is, per Richard Brody, the “greatest American political movie,” a truth-seeking frontier tale about the free press, vigilantism, and the myth of the American male.
To celebrate the release of a new book on filmmaker Matías Piñeiro (
Viola
), The Originals is proud to present a 35mm print of John Ford’s
The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
, a film that Piñeiro writes about. Published by Fireflies Press and Batalha – Centro de cinema,
From where do you start when drawing a flower?
is composed of Piñeiro’s notebooks, sketches, photographs, writings, and merges his filmmaking practice with his cinephilia as well as his longstanding work as a film educator.
Writes Piñeiro: “As flowers are a motif in the title of my book, I could not help but think about one of the most beautiful flowers in film history: the cactus flower in
The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
by John Ford. The beauty of this flower may reside in its extraordinary power for evoking a certain feeling of irrecoverable loss, a scar we have to learn to live with. This flower will be screened in a beautiful 35mm black and white print, as it was meant to be. The lack of color does something to this flower—we can’t learn all about it; we cannot fully pick it. It escapes us just in front of our faces but remains glowing within us.”
From where do you start when drawing a flower?
(Fireflies Press and Batalha – Centro de cinema)

records.description:
Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1953. 62 mins. 35mm. With Frank Silvera, Paul Mazursky, Kenneth Harp, Steve Coit, Virginia Leith. Kubrick’s first feature was long unavailable to the public before its revival at the 1993 Telluride Film Festival and subsequent restoration in 2010. Begun when Kubrick was just 23,
this allegory of war follows four soldiers who capture and torment an innocent peasant girl behind enemy lines. Made for $10,000 raised from friends and family with a script written by high school classmate and future Pulitzer Prize–winner Howard Sackler, this formally and practically inventive film is impressive enough to have earned the admiration of James Agee, even if Kubrick himself would later dismiss it as “amateur.”
Preceded by Kubrick’s 1951 documentary shorts
Day of the Fight
(16 mins, 35mm) and
Flying Padre
(9 mins, 35mm)
,
his first films, which show the influence of his years working as a New York photographer.

records.title: Meet Me in St. Louis
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1944, 113 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Judy Garland, Margaret O’Brien, Mary Astor, Leon Ames, Lucille Bremer, Tom Drake. In Minnelli’s bittersweet turn-of-the-century tale, his first color film and one of the greatest musicals ever made, a family contends with life, love, and an impending move from St. Louis to New York City. Featuring extended Halloween and Christmas sequences that place it firmly within multiple holiday movie canons, the whip-smart wry and gorgeously sentimental
Meet Me in St. Louis
is an endlessly rewatchable treasure that cemented the popularity of integrated narrative and music in American movies.

records.title: Liza Double Feature: Liza with a Z + The Sterile Cuckoo
records.description:
Liza with a Z
Dir. Bob Fosse, 1972, 55 mins. U.S. DCP. With Liza Minnelli. In 1972, everything was coming up Liza. Just three months after the February release of Bob Fosse’s masterpiece
Cabaret
(which would earn her an Academy Award for her instantly legendary starring performance), Minnelli and Fosse reteamed for
Liza with a Z
.
This concert for television, shot at New York’s Lyceum Theatre by Fosse and his
Cabaret
cinematographer Owen Roizman on eight 16mm cameras, edited by Alan Heim (who would go on to cut
All That Jazz
), with music coordination by Marvin Hamlisch (three years before
A Chorus Line
), is a monumental testament to the indefatigable spirit and musical gifts of this timeless, larger-than-life performer. From her tongue-twisting rendition of the title tune to the deliriously choreographed toe-tapper “Ring Them Bells” to the climactic
Cabaret
medley,
Liza with a Z
is an overwhelming showcase for her thrilling talents that won four Emmys.
The Sterile Cuckoo
Dir. Alan J. Pakula. 1969, 107 mins. U.S. 16mm. With Liza Minnelli, Wendell Burton, Tim McIntire. We’re pleased to pair
Liza with a Z
—Minnelli at her most fabulously in the spotlight—with her dramatic breakthrough role in Alan J. Pakula’s deeply moving, idiosyncratic late sixties love story, for which Minnelli earned an Best Actress Oscar nomination. She plays Mary Ann, aka “Pookie,” an emotionally forthright outcast who falls hard for fellow college student Jerry (Burton). As their romance deepens, so does her desperation. Pakula’s film reveals a core of melancholy beneath its initially comic exterior, while Minnelli is the main event in her first leading movie performance, announcing her gifts for embodying singularly quirky yet effortlessly layered women.

records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1962, 153 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Glenn Ford, Ingrid Thulin, Charles Boyer, Paul Henreid. According to French critic Jean Douchet,
The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse
was, at the time of release, Minnelli’s “most important film to date . . . it sums up and surpasses what went before, as

, for example, does for Hitchcock.” Adapted from the novel by Vicente Blasco Ibáñez, earlier made into the silent Valentino classic by Rex Ingram, this dreamlike and unusual production was updated to the World War II era and shot partly on location in Paris. The film stars Glenn Ford as an Argentinean cattle rancher who moves to Europe in the late 1930s, ultimately joining the French Resistance. Though in its day the film was a critical and commercial flop at a fragile moment for MGM, the historical complexities and technical achievements of this late Minnelli epic are undeniable.

In the years since its release, this ludicrously entertaining adaptation of the classic whodunit has become a beloved mainstay of eighties cinema. Its comedy all-star cast is headed by the brilliant Tim Curry as the butler of a mansion, where a group of strangers (Mr. Mustard, Mrs. Peacock, etc.) have been summoned under mysterious circumstances and must end up trying to solve a murder—or two.
Clue

records.description:
Dir. John Hughes. 1986, 103 mins. U.S. DCP. With Matthew Broderick, Alan Ruck, Mia Sara, Jeffrey Jones, Jennifer Grey. Beloved by his peers, loathed by his long-suffering dean, the ever-popular suburban high-school huckster Ferris Bueller (Matthew Broderick, at his very best) decides to skip class one glorious day, coercing his tight-ass best friend, Cameron Frye (Alan Ruck) and too-cool-for-school girlfriend (Mia Sara) to join him on an outing to Chicago. After nine absences, Dean Rooney knows something fishy is going on. However, Ferris’s motives aren’t all selfish: over the course of the day, he teaches Cameron a thing or two about independence. John Hughes’s hilarious hit walks the line between the slapstick and the poignant, with one unforgettable set piece after another. Special MVP shout-out to scowling Jennifer Grey as Ferris’s resentful sister Jeanie, who has her own crucial subplot. [Rated PG-13]

Say Anything…
stars a charismatic John Cusack as average student Lloyd Dobler, who pursues his class’s beautiful valedictorian Diane Court (Ione Skye), despite their differences in class and ambition. Meanwhile, Diane must reckon with a rising disillusionment towards her adoring father (John Mahoney), who has secrets of his own. Modest in scope yet deeply felt,

has proven to be a cornerstone of eighties American moviemaking, full of heartfelt pragmatism and snappy, memorable dialogue.

records.title: Stand by Me
records.description:
Dir. Rob Reiner. 1986, 90 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Wil Wheaton, River Phoenix, Corey Feldman, Jerry O’Connell, Kiefer Sutherland. Adapting Stephen King’s novella
The Body

Rob Reiner fashioned a mesmerizing and poignant tribute to the beauties and difficulties of growing up, following four tight-knit friends in the Pacific Northwest over one fateful weekend in 1959. Having heard a rumor that a peer of theirs was struck by a train and killed, the boys set off to find the body. What begins as a thoughtless lark becomes something transformative. One of Reiner’s greatest films, buoyed by a soundtrack of late fifties, early sixties hits and starring a remarkable young cast, including River Phoenix in his breakout role,
Stand by Me
is more than a work of nostalgia, it’s a true generational rite of passage. [Rated R]

records.title: Risky Business
records.description:

Risky Business,
following a series of mostly brainless early ’80s sex comedies and first-love dramas, was its sexual sophistication and sharp commentary on the growing capitalist mania of the Reagan era. As Joel Goodsen, who goes from sexually frustrated teen to entrepreneur pimp in the space of a weekend while his parents are away, Cruise offers a pure, embryonic dose of the singular charms that would define a decade, while De Mornay kills her every scene as the streetwise sex worker who becomes his accomplice

records.title: Brigadoon
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1954, 108 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Gene Kelly, Cyd Charisse, Van Johnson, Elaine Stewart. One of the first Cinemascope, Technicolor musicals, this MGM extravaganza, adapted from the stage by the great Lerner and Loewe, is an enchanting fantasy in which a pair of New Yorkers find themselves in a magical Scottish town called Brigadoon, which only materializes once every hundred years. No inhabitant of the town can cross the border to leave, or else the town will disappear—but a stranger can stay if he falls in love with someone there. Of course, complications ensue when Gene Kelly’s Tommy finds himself pining for the beautiful Fiona (Cyd Charisse). Featuring splendidly beautiful dance sequences and gorgeous set design,
Brigadoon
is a poignant supernatural romance about the aching ephemerality of existence.

records.title: I Dood It
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1943, 103 mins. U.S. 16mm. With Red Skelton, Eleanor Powell, Lena Horne, Hazel Scott, Jimmy Dorsey, Richard Ainley. One of Minnelli’s true oddball works, this WWII-era homefront entertainment mixes comedy, thriller, and musical revue in an unofficial remake of a Buster Keaton silent film called
Spite Marriage.
Right after his breakthrough hit
Cabin in the Sky
,
Minnelli was handed this troubled production—which had lost its original director during shooting—which somehow concerns both a backstage love affair and foiled Nazi saboteurs. But Minnelli put his signature touch on it, especially in the musical sequences, the best of which, featuring his
Cabin
co-
star Lena Horne in a “song battle” with the great jazz pianist Hazel Scott, both performing with an all-Black chorus and band, is worth the price of admission.

records.title: The Pirate
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1948, 102 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Judy Garland, Gene Kelly, Walter Slezak. One of Minnelli’s most purely enjoyable movies, this high-energy musical comedy is an endless hall of mirrors that gives Judy Garland and Gene Kelly two of their funniest roles, allowing him to show off his dazzling athletic prowess and her to flaunt her comic genius in scene after scene. One of the great Freed Unit entertainments—and one of its most decidedly queer texts—
The Pirate
follows Garland’s frustrated, betrothed Manuela, who wants to escape from her daily drudgery and boring fiancé into a fantasy world and be whisked away by the romantic pirate Macoco. However, the assumed Macoco (played by Kelly) is actually an actor in disguise, while the real Macoco is hidden in plain sight. Wild plot turnabouts abound, as do some of Kelly’s most remarkable physicals feats, in this nonstop Technicolor delight.

records.title: Cabin in the Sky
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1943, 98 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Ethel Waters, Eddie “Rochester” Anderson, Lena Horne, John Bubbles, Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington and His Orchestra. After years of advising, assisting edits, and directing standalone musical numbers for Arthur Freed’s soon-to-be legendary MGM musicals production unit, Minnelli was entrusted with directing his first feature, and he officially burst out of the gate with the surprise smash
Cabin in the Sky
. Featuring an all-Black cast, during a period when African American performers were increasingly vocal in demanding better representation in entertainment,
Cabin in the Sky
was a risky venture, as theaters in the racist South would refuse to screen it. Elsewhere it was a sensation, a jazz-tinged musical comedy drama—starring Eddie “Rochester” Anderson as a gambler arguing for his soul at the pearly gates after he is shot during a craps game—often credited as the first truly “integrated” film, in terms of how the songs are built into the narrative. Ethel Waters and Lena Horne are singing standouts as the angelic wife and sultry mistress perched on each of his shoulders.

records.title: The Bad and the Beautiful
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1952, 118 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Kirk Douglas, Lana Turner, Dick Powell, Gloria Grahame. Two years after
All About Eve
,
Minnelli directed this similarly barbed poison pen to show business, though the target this time was Hollywood. Douglas stars in one of his nastiest roles as the detestable, cynical producer Jonathan Shields, remembered with zero fondness by lovers and colleagues in an invigorating flashback structure. One of Minnelli’s greatest melodramas—and one of the most caustic films Tinseltown ever made about itself—
The Bad and the Beautiful
won five Academy Awards, for its screenplay, cinematography, art direction, costume design, and best supporting actress for Gloria Grahame in a small but memorable role.

records.title: Lust for Life
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1956, 122 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Kirk Douglas, Anthony Quinn, James Donald, Pamela Brown, Everett Sloane. This extraordinarily vivid, Technicolor biopic about the life and art of Vincent Van Gogh is among Minnelli’s greatest visual achievements. Kirk Douglas received an Oscar nomination for Best Actor as a mythic, tortured incarnation of Van Gogh, while Anthony Quinn won Best Supporting Actor for his earthy, unforgettable turn as his friend and fellow carouser Paul Gauguin. With its gorgeous widescreen compositions, sometimes taken over by Van Gogh’s canvases,
Lust for Life
is an enveloping melodrama about two of the director’s recurring preoccupations: the creation of art and the trappings of masculinity.

records.title: Madame Bovary
records.description:
Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1949, 114 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Jennifer Jones, James Mason, Van Heflin, Louis Jourdan. Minnelli’s improbably stunning rendition of Gustav Flaubert’s oft-adapted classic novel casts Oscar-winner Jennifer Jones as Emma Bovary, the provincial doctor’s wife whose pursuit of romance and social status lead to financial ruination and tragedy. Lavishly mounted and emotionally penetrating, this Hollywood rendition of the eternally controversial tale of adultery was called by the great critic Robin Wood “perhaps the most neglected and misrecognized of [Minnelli’s] major works” and features some of Minnelli’s most astounding camerawork, especially during a virtuoso mirrored ballroom sequence that one will never forget.

records.title: Garden to Table: Cure a Vegetable and Make a Pie
records.description:
If you’ve ever wondered how to incorporate veggie-growing techniques into your backyard or community garden, or what vegetables are in season this month (and want a little inspiration for how to cook them), this class is a fun way to find out. You’ll learn about producing your own food from seedling to plate, and taste the flavors of each season. This class is ideal for the home cook, gardener (or aspiring gardener), or even someone whose New Year’s resolution is to eat more vegetables than last year.
During this time of the year there is little left growing on the farm, but there are still vegetables to be eaten!
The vegetable stars of this class are winter squash, pumpkins, potatoes, and sweet potatoes. You’ll take home either pumpkin, squash, or sweet potatoes as well as recipes for pumpkin pie, sweet potato pie, and a savory squash or sweet potato dish.

records.title: Meet our Animals: Friendly Finewool Sheep
records.description:
Calling all animal lovers and future zoologists!
Join our 2026 Meet the Animals series to get up close with the furry, feathered, and four-legged residents of our farm! We’ll get up close and personal to observe and learn lots about our animal buddies, from their unique behaviors and other fun facts! Get ready for a hands-on animal adventure that will deepen your connection to the creatures we share our world with.

records.title: Grow & Gather: Family Gardening Program
records.description:
Learn how to plant seedlings, directly sow, weed, prune, companion plant, harvest vegetables, dry herbs, and more with Queens County Farm Museum’s in-house Botanist and biology expert, Tess Fleming. Our Compost and STEM Coordinators will also be onsite for several of these fully outdoor, hands-on gardening sessions. Sessions take place in one or more of our six Teaching Gardens where we plant and harvest tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, a wide variety of lettuces, kale, broccoli, zucchini, summer squash, sunflowers, strawberries, onions, potatoes, turnips, parsnips, green beans, snap peas, cucamelons, radishes, carrots, watermelon, and a large assortment of herbs and spices.
Each session is 1 hour long and focuses on a particular topic related to gardening:
– Visiting the teaching gardens and discovering the plants grown in each area
– Tasting plant-based dishes based around seasonal produce
– A hands-on gardening activity related to plant or animal care on the farm
– Preparing a dish for you to take home to cook or bake along with recipes
What could be better? Learn new skills, get your hands dirty, take a walk outdoors, and eat the freshest produce available!

records.title: Jewelry Making Basics
records.description:
Unleash your creativity and learn the art of jewelry design in this fun, hands-on three-part series with Laura Graney, an accomplished jewelry designer whose work has been featured at the Teen Choice Awards, Country Music Awards, and in magazines and boutiques throughout the East Coast.
Explore the beauty and versatility of semi-precious stones, sterling silver, freshwater pearls, Swarovski and other crystals, while learning essential jewelry-making techniques including wire wrapping, shaping, connecting, and finishing. You’ll also work with stainless steel wire for practice, giving you the opportunity to build confidence with the tools and techniques before creating your finished pieces.
Throughout the series, you’ll design and take home four unique pieces of jewelry: a stylish cocktail ring, a wire-wrapped ring featuring semi-precious stones and crystals, a bracelet incorporating beautiful stones and/or pearls, and a pair of earrings embellished with crystals or freshwater pearls.
Whether you’re completely new to jewelry making or looking to develop your skills, this series offers a creative and approachable introduction to designing jewelry you’ll be proud to wear or gift.
Bring your own tools and supplies, or purchase a materials kit during the first class for an additional fee.

records.title: Book Launch at Columbus Circle: The Fair Fields: My Way to Words by Rosanna Warren in conversation with Margo Jefferson
records.description:
About
the Book.
A memoir-in-vignettes recalling a poet’s early years and memories from a literary household.
More than a consecutive memoir,
The Fair Fields
presents a set of linked vignettes about what it was like to grow up in a white, liberal, literary household in Connecticut in the 1950s and early 1960s. Readers will meet characters they probably recognize, including Rosanna Warren’s parents—writers Robert Penn Warren and Eleanor Clark—and their friends: authors, visual artists, musicians, editors, and publishers.
The narrative tracks Rosanna’s early childhood to young womanhood, taking in along the way visions of neolithic Brittany, Roman ruins in southern France, the French Revolution, the Algerian War, and the throes of the American civil rights movement in the 1960s. As much as a personal story, it’s a set of portraits from a certain gallery of post–World War II American intellectual life. It also tells the tale of a young artist finding her way from painting, her first vocation, to a life in writing.
About the Author.
Rosanna Warren
is the author of
Hindsight
and six previous volumes of poetry and is a professor emerita in the John U. Nef Committee on Social Thought at the University of Chicago. She is a recipient of awards from the Academy of American Poets and the American Academy of Arts and Letters, among others. She lives in New York City.
About the Moderator.
Margo Jefferson
is a memoirist and critic. She has published three books: Constructing a Nervous System, Negroland, and On Michael Jackson. She has been a staff critic for The New York Times and Newsweek, and her reviews have been widely published and anthologized. She received a Pulitzer Prize for her criticism, a National Book Critics Circle Award for Negroland, and a Windham Campbell Prize
for nonfiction. She teaches at Columbia University.

records.title: Family History Month Workshop 2: Transcribe-a-thon
records.venue_name: Staten Island Museum at Snug Harbor
records.venue_address: 1000 Richmond Terrace Building A, Staten Island, NY 10301
records.description:
Free with museum admission.
Help the Staten Island Museum transcribe newly digitized family history records, making them more easily searchable and accessible for researchers. A transcribe-a-thon is an event where people gather to work simultaneously on a transcription project. No previous experience is required. Training and snacks will be provided. Bring your own laptop or tablet.
This program is part of the museum’s
Access Collaboration and Equity in Genealogy Initiative (ACEGen)
. ACEGen endeavors to document and make publicly accessible records from communities that have been underrepresented in historical institutional collecting. ACEGen fosters collaboration between repositories, organizations, and the public to improve access and equity in Staten Island’s family history records. These programs are supported by the New York Community Trust and the Altman Foundation.
